entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To change something, usually slightly, so that it is different but keeps its basic form.
entries.usage: A little more formal than *change* and common in writing and news: *alter a plan*, *alter the course of something*, *life-altering*, *digitally altered*. In everyday American English it is also the normal word for changing the fit of clothes: *get a dress altered*, *alterations*. It sounds exactly like *altar*, the table in a church.
entries.pattern: alter a plan / a document / the course of something; have clothes altered
examples: The tailor can **alter** the jacket so the sleeves aren't so long.
One semester abroad **altered** the course of Mia's life.
Police say the photo was digitally **altered** before it was shared online.

drill.sentence: My wedding dress was two sizes too big, so I had it {{altered}} at a little shop near my office.
drill.hint: changed to fit better (not *tailored*, *fixed* or *taken in*)

entries.related: *change* — the general everyday word; *modify* — change something to improve it, more technical; *adjust* — change slightly so that something works or fits.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To pull out of a race, competition, agreement or place; or to officially take back an offer, request or statement.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and formal situations: *withdraw from a race / a tournament / a deal*. With a direct object it means take back: *withdraw an offer / an application / a complaint / a remark*. It is more formal than *pull out* and *take back*; the past forms are *withdrew* and *withdrawn*.
entries.pattern: withdraw from + race / deal / competition; withdraw an offer / application / comment
examples: After hurting her knee in training, Dana had to **withdraw** from the marathon.
The buyers **withdrew** their offer on the house after the inspection found mold in the basement.
The coach later **withdrew** his comments about the referee and apologized.

drill.sentence: The city {{withdrew}} from the stadium deal after the developer missed two deadlines.
drill.hint: formally pulled out (one word; not *backed out*)

entries.related: *pull out (of)* — the everyday equivalent; *back out (of)* — informal, break a promise or deal; *retract* — take back a statement, more formal.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To notice or discover something that is hard to see, hear, smell or measure, often with a device or a careful test.
entries.usage: Common in medicine, science, security and news: *detect cancer early*, *detect a gas leak*, *detect fraud*; the passive is frequent (*no trace was detected*). In conversation it is used for subtle signals in people, often humorously: *Do I detect a hint of jealousy?* It is more formal than *notice* or *spot*.
entries.pattern: detect a leak / a disease / fraud / a change; detect a hint / note of + feeling
examples: The test can **detect** the disease years before any symptoms appear.
Do I **detect** a hint of sarcasm in that “congratulations”?
Our smoke alarm is so sensitive that it **detects** toast burning two rooms away.

drill.sentence: Airport scanners are designed to {{detect}} metal objects hidden under clothing.
drill.hint: notice something that is hard to see (not *find*, *spot* or *pick up*)

entries.related: *notice* — everyday, often by chance; *spot* — see something, informal; *identify* — say exactly what something is.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Unusually good, much better than average; or unusual and not typical, so that normal rules may not apply.
entries.usage: As praise it is stronger than *very good* and common in reference letters, reviews and awards: *an exceptional student*, *exceptional service*. The second sense appears mainly in the formal phrases *in exceptional circumstances* and *in exceptional cases*, typical of rules and policies. The adverb is frequent before adjectives: *exceptionally warm*, *exceptionally talented*.
entries.pattern: an exceptional student / talent / meal; in exceptional circumstances / cases
examples: Marcus is an **exceptional** pianist; at fourteen he was already playing with the city orchestra.
Because of her surgery, the school treated it as an **exceptional** case and let her take the exam in June.
The food was fine, but the service was truly **exceptional**.

drill.sentence: Hotel staff can waive the cancellation fee, but only in {{exceptional}} circumstances like a medical emergency.
drill.hint: out of the ordinary (not *special*, *unusual*, *extraordinary* or *extenuating*)

entries.related: *outstanding* — excellent, close to the praise sense; *extraordinary* — very unusual or remarkable; *exceptionally* — the adverb: *exceptionally talented*.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To change something completely, in its form, appearance or character, usually so that it becomes much better.
entries.usage: Much stronger than *change*: it suggests a dramatic, complete difference, often in *transform A into B* or *transform the way people do something*. It is very common in business and tech talk (*digital transformation*, *transformative*), where it can sound like hype. For places and lives it is warm and positive: *The new park has transformed the neighborhood*.
entries.pattern: transform A into B; transform the way / how people + verb; completely transform
examples: A coat of paint and some new lamps **transformed** the dark basement into a cozy family room.
Having a baby completely **transformed** the way Josh thinks about money.
Smartphones have **transformed** how people shop, date and find their way around cities.

drill.sentence: Moving to the coast has completely {{transformed}} my dad; he's relaxed, tan and finally sleeping well.
drill.hint: made a totally different person of (not *changed*)

entries.related: *change* — the general word; *convert* — change something for a new use (*convert a garage into an office*); *revolutionize* — change completely, even stronger.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not large in size, amount or value; or, about a person, not talking much about their own abilities or success.
entries.usage: The size sense is common in news and business as a neutral, polite word for *small*: *a modest increase / income / house / budget*. About people it is praise: *She's very modest about her achievements*. *Don't be so modest!* is a friendly reply when someone plays down their success.
entries.pattern: a modest increase / income / house; be modest about something
examples: Despite winning three Olympic medals, Ellie is very **modest** and rarely mentions them.
They live in a **modest** two-bedroom house at the edge of town.
Bus fares will see a **modest** increase of about three percent next year.

drill.sentence: Oh, don't be so {{modest}}; your speech was the best part of the whole wedding.
drill.hint: quick to play down your own success (not *humble*)

entries.related: *humble* — modest, also suggests simple or low status (*humble beginnings*); *moderate* — not extreme, for amounts and views; *boastful* — the opposite of the second sense.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A general feeling or opinion about something, especially one shared by many people; also the kind feeling behind words or a gift.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and polls: *public sentiment*, *consumer / investor sentiment*, *the sentiment among staff*. In conversation, *I appreciate the sentiment* means *thank you for the kind thought*, and *I share that sentiment* means *I agree*. Do not confuse it with *sentimentality* (too much tender emotion), which goes with the adjective *sentimental*.
entries.pattern: public / consumer / investor sentiment; sentiment among + group; appreciate the sentiment
examples: Public **sentiment** turned against the new parking fees within a few weeks.
It's only a twenty-dollar gift card, but I really appreciate the **sentiment**.
Among the nurses, the **sentiment** was clear: they wanted fewer night shifts, not higher pay.

drill.sentence: Consumer {{sentiment}} fell sharply in March, with most people telling pollsters they expected prices to keep rising.
drill.hint: the general mood and opinion of shoppers (not *confidence* or *optimism*)

entries.related: *feeling* — the everyday word; *mood* — a general, often temporary feeling; *sentimental* — adjective, showing (too much) tender emotion.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A set of beliefs and ideas, especially political or economic ones, that shapes how a group sees society and how it thinks things should be.
entries.usage: Used in news, history and academic writing: *political ideology*, *the dominant ideology*, *a clash of ideologies*. In everyday debate, *ideological* and *driven by ideology* are usually critical: they suggest that someone follows fixed beliefs rather than facts. Americans say both *eye-dee-AH-luh-jee* and *id-ee-AH-luh-jee*.
entries.pattern: political / economic ideology; driven by ideology; a clash of ideologies
examples: The documentary shows how a lonely teenager was slowly drawn into an extremist **ideology** online.
As mayor, Rosa is a pragmatist; she cares more about fixing potholes than about **ideology**.
Some people treat their diet almost like an **ideology**, with strict rules and no exceptions.

drill.sentence: Communism and fascism were rival political {{ideologies}} that divided Europe for much of the twentieth century.
drill.hint: sets of beliefs about how society should work (not *movements* or *systems*)

entries.related: *doctrine* — the official beliefs of a group; *worldview* — a personal way of seeing the world; *ideological* — adjective, often critical.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In a way that suits the situation just described; or, at the start of a sentence, therefore, as a result.
entries.usage: In the first sense it comes after the verb (*plan / dress / act / adjust accordingly*) and is common in everyday instructions and emails. At the start of a sentence it means *therefore*; this use is formal and mostly written, in reports, legal texts and official letters. Do not confuse it with *according to*, which introduces a source.
entries.pattern: verb + accordingly (plan / dress / adjust accordingly); Accordingly, + clause (formal)
examples: The forecast says it'll be windy and cold on the trail, so dress **accordingly**.
Interest rates went up, and our monthly mortgage payment rose **accordingly**.
The bridge failed its safety inspection. **Accordingly**, it will stay closed until repairs are finished.

drill.sentence: Forty people have said yes instead of twenty, so we'll need to order food {{accordingly}}.
drill.hint: to match the new situation (not *appropriately*)

mistake.wrong: Accordingly to the forecast, it will rain tomorrow.
mistake.right: According to the forecast, it will rain tomorrow.
mistake.why: *According to* introduces a source; the adverb *accordingly* never does.

entries.related: *therefore* — formal, more common for logical steps; *as a result* — neutral linking phrase; *appropriately* — in a suitable way, without pointing back to a situation.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Used before a name or label to show that this is what people call something, often because you think the name is wrong or not deserved.
entries.usage: Often skeptical or sarcastic: *my so-called friends* means they don't behave like friends. It can be neutral before a technical term (*the so-called Goldilocks zone*), but listeners may still hear doubt, so use *known as* or *called* when you simply want to name something. German *sogenannt* is usually neutral, so German speakers can sound more critical than they intend.
entries.pattern: so-called + noun (before the name or label)
examples: My **so-called** best friend didn't even text me on my birthday.
The **so-called** luxury apartment turned out to be a basement with one tiny window.
Earth sits in the **so-called** Goldilocks zone, where a planet is neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water.

drill.sentence: Our {{so-called}} express shuttle took two hours to get us from the hotel to the airport.
drill.hint: named this, though the name doesn't fit (not *supposed*)

entries.related: *supposed* — believed or said to be true, often doubted (*the supposed shortcut*); *self-styled* — named so by oneself, critical; *known as* — neutral naming.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Giving good results or value for the amount of money spent.
entries.usage: Common in business, government and health reports: *a cost-effective way to*, *a cost-effective solution*, *more cost-effective than*. It is about value, not only a low price: a cheap option that breaks quickly is not cost-effective. It is hyphenated in front of a noun and usually after a verb too (*It's more cost-effective*).
entries.pattern: a cost-effective way / solution / option; more cost-effective than + noun / -ing
examples: Buying one good winter coat is more **cost-effective** than replacing a cheap one every year.
For short trips around town, an e-bike is a surprisingly **cost-effective** way to commute.
Insulating old school buildings is one of the most **cost-effective** ways for the city to cut its energy bills.

drill.sentence: Instead of hiring a full-time designer, the café found it more {{cost-effective}} to pay a freelancer for each project.
drill.hint: better value for the money (not *economical*, *efficient* or *affordable*)

entries.related: *economical* — using little money, fuel or energy; *affordable* — cheap enough for people to buy; *bang for your buck* — informal American phrase for good value.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very serious or severe; used for problems, shortages and pain that are happening now and need attention.
entries.usage: Typical partners are *an acute shortage (of)*, *acute pain*, *an acute crisis*, and the adverb in *acutely aware*. In medicine, *acute* means sudden and short-term, the opposite of *chronic*. German *akut* is wider: for *Das ist nicht akut*, English says *That's not urgent*.
entries.pattern: an acute shortage of + noun; acute pain / anxiety; an acute problem / crisis
examples: There's an **acute** shortage of nurses in rural hospitals, so some wards have closed.
Jake went to the ER with **acute** pain in his lower right side.
The housing problem became **acute** when two big employers moved to town in the same year.

drill.sentence: The drought has caused an {{acute}} shortage of drinking water in several villages.
drill.hint: very severe and pressing (not *alarming* or *extreme*)

entries.related: *severe* — very bad, more general; *chronic* — long-lasting, the opposite in medicine; *dire* — extremely serious, often about need or consequences.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Having a special quality, look, sound, smell or taste that makes someone or something easy to recognize and different from others.
entries.usage: Neutral or positive, used for voices, styles, smells, flavors and designs: *a distinctive voice / style / smell / flavor*. Do not confuse it with *distinct*, which means clearly separate or clearly noticeable (*two distinct groups*, *a distinct smell of gas*). *Distinguished* is different again: respected, or looking dignified.
entries.pattern: a distinctive voice / style / smell / flavor / look; distinctive features
examples: Even on a bad phone line, I recognized Grandma's **distinctive** laugh right away.
Smoked paprika gives the stew its **distinctive** flavor.
The architect's buildings are **distinctive**: white curved walls and huge round windows.

drill.sentence: With its red brick tower and green clock face, the old train station has a very {{distinctive}} look.
drill.hint: easy to recognize because it's unlike others (not *unique* or *recognizable*)

mistake.wrong: The two words have distinctive meanings.
mistake.right: The two words have distinct meanings.
mistake.why: *Distinct* means clearly different or separate; *distinctive* means easy to recognize because of a special feature.

entries.related: *characteristic* — typical of a person or thing; *unique* — the only one of its kind; *nondescript* — the opposite, ordinary and forgettable.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: The most modern and advanced, using the newest ideas, methods or technology.
entries.usage: Common in business, tech, medicine and advertising: *cutting-edge technology / research / design / treatment*. It is hyphenated before a noun; the noun phrase *at the cutting edge (of)* has no hyphen. On company websites it is so common that it can sound like empty hype.
entries.pattern: cutting-edge technology / research / design; at the cutting edge of + field
examples: The new children's hospital has **cutting-edge** equipment that most small clinics can't afford.
Their kitchen looks old-fashioned, but all the appliances are **cutting-edge**.
The company makes **cutting-edge** batteries for electric trucks and buses.

drill.sentence: The museum uses {{cutting-edge}} virtual reality so visitors can walk through ancient Rome.
drill.hint: the most advanced available (not *state-of-the-art* or *the latest*)

entries.related: *state-of-the-art* — very close, a bit more formal; *leading-edge* — similar, in business; *outdated* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Based on the results of scientific research and evidence, rather than on habit, tradition or personal opinion.
entries.usage: Standard in medicine, public health, education and policy: *evidence-based medicine / practice / treatment / policy*. It signals seriousness and approval, and organizations use it to show that they follow research, not trends. It is hyphenated before a noun; in casual talk people say *backed by research* or *proven*.
entries.pattern: evidence-based medicine / treatment / practice / policy / approach
examples: Before you buy that detox tea, look for **evidence-based** advice from a doctor, not an influencer.
The school replaced its old reading program with an **evidence-based** approach to teaching phonics.
The city says its new traffic rules are **evidence-based**, using crash data from other cities.

drill.sentence: Modern {{evidence-based}} medicine asks doctors to choose treatments that have been tested in careful clinical trials.
drill.hint: relying on proof from studies, the standard term in medicine (not *scientific* or *science-backed*)

entries.related: *research-based* — similar, common in education; *data-driven* — guided by data, common in business and tech; *anecdotal* — based on personal stories, the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Involving a lot of risk, because a great deal can be won or lost depending on the result.
entries.usage: Mostly used before nouns: *a high-stakes game / negotiation / exam / decision*. It is common in news, sports and business, and *high-stakes testing* is a standard term in US education for exams that decide graduation, admission or school funding. After a verb, people usually say *the stakes are high*.
entries.pattern: a high-stakes game / meeting / exam / decision; the stakes are high
examples: Choosing a college felt like a **high-stakes** decision at seventeen, as if my whole future depended on it.
The two companies are in **high-stakes** talks that could decide the future of three thousand jobs.
A penalty kick in the last minute of a World Cup final is about as **high-stakes** as sports get.

drill.sentence: The bar exam is a {{high-stakes}} test: if Leo fails, he loses the job offer from the law firm.
drill.hint: with a lot riding on the result (not *make-or-break*)

entries.related: *make-or-break* — deciding success or failure; *risky* — involving danger or possible loss; *low-stakes* — the opposite, nothing important depends on it.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The great size, extent or importance of something, especially a problem, task or event.
entries.usage: Common in news and serious speech: *the magnitude of the problem / task / disaster*, *the sheer magnitude*. *Of this magnitude* means *this big* (*a project of this magnitude*). In science it is also a measure of size, as in an earthquake's *magnitude* and *an order of magnitude* (about ten times).
entries.pattern: the (sheer) magnitude of + problem / task; of this / such magnitude; an order of magnitude
examples: We didn't grasp the **magnitude** of the flooding until we saw the photos from the air.
A wedding of this **magnitude** takes at least a year to plan.
The new chip is an order of **magnitude** faster than the old one.

drill.sentence: Moving Dad into a nursing home was a decision of such {{magnitude}} that the whole family met to talk it through.
drill.hint: great size and seriousness (not *importance*, *significance*, *weight* or *gravity*)

entries.related: *scale* — size or extent, more neutral; *extent* — how far something reaches; *enormity* — the great seriousness of something bad.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The state of being healthy, happy and comfortable, both in body and in mind.
entries.usage: Common in health, HR, school and news contexts: *mental / emotional well-being*, *the well-being of children*, *employee well-being*. It sounds caring but a little official; in conversation people often say *health* or *how someone is doing*. American writing usually keeps the hyphen; *wellbeing* without it is more common in British English.
entries.pattern: mental / physical / emotional well-being; the well-being of + person / group
examples: Regular sleep and exercise matter as much for your mental **well-being** as for your body.
The new office has quiet rooms and walking paths to support employee **well-being**.
The judge said her only concern was the children's **well-being**.

drill.sentence: Pets can do a lot for the {{well-being}} of older people who live alone.
drill.hint: overall state of being healthy and content (not *health*, *happiness* or *welfare*)

entries.related: *welfare* — health and safety, often official (*child welfare*); *wellness* — American, an active effort to stay healthy (*wellness programs*); *happiness* — a feeling, narrower.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To balance one effect, cost or amount with an opposite one, so that the overall result changes less or stays the same.
entries.usage: Common in business, finance and news: *offset the cost / the losses / the increase*, often passive with *by*: *Higher prices were partly offset by lower fuel costs*. The past and past participle are also *offset*. *Carbon offsets* are payments meant to balance the emissions you cause, for example on a flight.
entries.pattern: offset A with B; A is (partly) offset by B; offset the cost / losses
examples: The higher rent will be partly **offset** by the money I save on gas now that I can walk to work.
The coffee shop raised its prices to **offset** the rising cost of beans and milk.
Strong online sales **offset** the drop in store visits during the holiday season.

drill.sentence: Selling our old car helped {{offset}} the cost of the new one, but we still needed a small loan.
drill.hint: partly balance out (one word; not *cover*, *lower* or *reduce*)

entries.related: *make up for* — compensate, more conversational; *cancel out* — balance completely so there is no effect; *counterbalance* — balance with an opposite force, more formal.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Of a rise or fall: very large and sudden. Of a price or fee: too high, more than seems fair.
entries.usage: News and business use *a steep rise / increase / drop / decline* for numbers, where *sharp* is a close synonym. About prices, *steep* is common in conversation and a bit informal: *That's a little steep*, *steep fees*. The basic meaning, about hills and stairs, gives the same image of going up or down quickly.
entries.pattern: a steep rise / drop / decline (in + noun); a steep price / fee; That's (a bit) steep
examples: Forty dollars for a burger and fries? That's a little **steep**.
There's been a **steep** rise in egg prices since bird flu hit several large farms.
The museum charges a **steep** entrance fee, but kids under twelve get in free.

drill.sentence: After the factory closed, the town saw a {{steep}} decline in population as young families moved away.
drill.hint: very large and fast (not *sharp*, *rapid* or *dramatic*)

entries.related: *sharp* — very close for rises and falls; *pricey* — informal, expensive; *gradual* — the opposite of a steep change.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To reveal something bad or hidden, such as a crime or a lie; or to put someone or something in a situation without protection from harm.
entries.usage: The first sense is common in journalism: *expose corruption / a scandal / a fraud*, *expose someone as a liar*. The second takes *to* and is often passive: *exposed to the sun / to risk / to toxic chemicals*. The related noun *exposé* (ek-spoh-ZAY) is a news report that reveals wrongdoing, unlike German *Exposé*, which is a summary or proposal.
entries.pattern: expose a scandal / a fraud / the truth; expose someone as + noun; be exposed to + danger
examples: A newspaper investigation **exposed** the charity's director, who had spent donations on luxury cars.
Firefighters were **exposed** to toxic smoke for hours while the warehouse burned.
Leaving your laptop unlocked in a café **exposes** your accounts to anyone who walks by.

drill.sentence: The documentary {{exposed}} the hidden dangers of the cheap phone chargers sold online.
drill.hint: brought into the open (not *revealed*, *uncovered* or *highlighted*)

entries.related: *reveal* — make known, neutral; *uncover* — discover something hidden; *shield* — protect, the opposite of the second sense.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Able to exist, work or live together without problems or conflict.
entries.usage: Used for people in relationships (*We just weren't compatible*), for devices and software (*compatible with older phones*) and for ideas or plans (*compatible with our goals*). The partner follows *with*; the opposite is *incompatible*. In tech, *backward-compatible* means that a new version still works with old ones.
entries.pattern: compatible with + noun; (not) fully compatible; incompatible
examples: They were great friends, but as roommates they weren't **compatible**; she's a night owl and he's up at five.
The new building plans aren't **compatible** with the historic character of the neighborhood.
A job with constant travel isn't really **compatible** with having a newborn at home.

drill.sentence: Some older games aren't {{compatible}} with the new console, so check the list before you trade yours in.
drill.hint: able to work together (not *usable* or *playable*)

entries.related: *suited (to)* — right for each other or for a purpose; *consistent with* — in agreement with facts or ideas; *incompatible* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make sure that people obey a law, rule or agreement, for example by checking them and punishing those who break it.
entries.usage: Common in news, law and everyday rules: *enforce a law / a rule / a ban / a contract / the speed limit*. Frequent partners are *strictly* and *rarely*: a rule can exist but *not be enforced*. *Law enforcement* is the standard American term for the police and similar agencies.
entries.pattern: enforce a law / rule / ban / curfew; strictly / rarely enforced
examples: The park has a no-dogs rule, but nobody really **enforces** it.
Police will strictly **enforce** the speed limit near schools starting next month.
The new manager is determined to **enforce** the dress code that everyone used to ignore.

drill.sentence: The library has a no-food policy, but the staff rarely {{enforce}} it unless someone brings in a whole pizza.
drill.hint: make people obey (not *apply* or *police*)

mistake.wrong: My boss enforced me to work on Sunday.
mistake.right: My boss forced me to work on Sunday.
mistake.why: *Enforce* takes a rule or law as its object; to make a person do something, use *force* or *make*.

entries.related: *impose* — introduce a rule, tax or punishment; *uphold* — keep a law or decision in force, formal; *crack down on* — start enforcing much more strictly.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To carry out a plan, task, strategy or order, especially in a skillful and organized way.
entries.usage: Common in business, sports and military language: *execute a plan / a strategy / a play*, *well-executed*, and in computing, *execute a program*. The noun is *execution*, as in *great idea, poor execution*. In everyday speech *carry out* or *pull off* is more common; remember that *execute* also means *put to death*.
entries.pattern: execute a plan / strategy / play / order; well / poorly executed
examples: The idea was great, but the team didn't **execute** it well, and the launch was a mess.
The quarterback **executed** the play perfectly, and they scored with ten seconds left.
The heist in the movie is so carefully **executed** that you almost cheer for the thieves.

drill.sentence: We had a clear plan for the surprise party; the hard part was {{executing}} it without Mom finding out.
drill.hint: putting into action, smoothly (not *implementing* or *organizing*)

entries.related: *carry out* — the everyday equivalent; *implement* — put a plan or system into effect, formal; *pull off* — informal, succeed at something difficult.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Language meant to persuade or impress people, often seen as insincere or empty because it is not backed by action.
entries.usage: In news and debate it is often critical: *empty rhetoric*, *heated rhetoric*, *the rhetoric doesn't match reality*. In schools and universities it is neutral: the study of persuasive speaking and writing. German *Rhetorik* is mostly neutral or positive, so calling a talk *just rhetoric* in English is much more critical than it may sound.
entries.pattern: empty / heated / campaign rhetoric; tone down the rhetoric
examples: The company says it puts customers first, but that's just **rhetoric**; the help line still makes you wait an hour.
Both coaches toned down their **rhetoric** before the rematch.
In college, Nina took a class on classical **rhetoric** and read Aristotle and Cicero.

drill.sentence: The landlord's promise of “luxury living” turned out to be empty {{rhetoric}}: the elevator hasn't worked since May.
drill.hint: persuasive language with nothing behind it (not *words*, *promises*, *hype* or *talk*)

entries.related: *spin* — presenting facts in a favorable way; *hype* — exaggerated promotion; *rhetorical question* — a question asked for effect, not for an answer.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: The best or most effective possible in a particular situation or for a particular purpose.
entries.usage: Common in science, medicine, business and tech: *optimal conditions / performance / results / temperature*, *the optimal time to*. In conversation it sounds technical; people usually say *best* or *ideal*. Because it already means *best*, careful writers avoid *most optimal* and *more optimal*, though both are heard.
entries.pattern: optimal conditions / performance / temperature / time; optimal for + noun
examples: The **optimal** temperature for storing wine is around fifty-five degrees Fahrenheit.
The pharmacist said the **optimal** time to take this pill is with breakfast.
The app finds the **optimal** route for a delivery driver with twenty stops.

drill.sentence: Tomatoes need at least six hours of direct sun a day for {{optimal}} growth.
drill.hint: as good as it can be, technical word (not *best*, *ideal*, *healthy* or *maximum*)

entries.related: *ideal* — perfect, more everyday; *optimum* — same meaning, also a noun (*the optimum*); *suboptimal* — less than ideal, often a polite understatement.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: What is usual or expected in a group or society; also a shared rule of behavior that most people follow.
entries.usage: Two patterns are common: *the norm* means what is normal (*Remote work is now the norm*), and *norms* means shared rules of behavior (*social / cultural norms*). Typical phrases are *become the norm* and *break with the norm*. German *Norm* also means an industrial or technical standard, which in English is a *standard*.
entries.pattern: the norm (in + place / group); become the norm; social / cultural norms
examples: In many homes, it's the **norm** to take your shoes off at the door.
One of our team **norms** is that nobody sends emails after 7 p.m.
Every family has its own unspoken **norms** about who cleans up after dinner.

drill.sentence: Video calls were rare at my company before 2020, but they quickly became the {{norm}}.
drill.hint: what is usual and expected (not *standard*, *default* or *rule*)

entries.related: *standard* — an agreed level of quality, also technical; *convention* — a traditional way of doing things; *the exception* — the opposite of *the norm*.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Having enough skill or knowledge to do something well, or at least to the required standard.
entries.usage: It is positive but modest: a *competent* doctor or mechanic does the job properly, not brilliantly, so it is weaker praise than German *kompetent*. In reviews, *perfectly competent* or *a competent performance* can be faint praise. Common patterns are *competent at* or *in* something and *competent to do* something; in law, *competent* means mentally able to make decisions.
entries.pattern: a competent driver / teacher / cook; competent at / in + skill; competent to + verb
examples: I'm a **competent** cook, but I'd never try to bake a wedding cake.
We need a **competent** plumber, not my brother-in-law with a YouTube video.
The movie is **competent** but forgettable; nothing in it surprised me.

drill.sentence: Alex isn't a brilliant driver, but he's {{competent}} enough to handle the highway in light snow.
drill.hint: able to do it to an acceptable standard (not *capable*, *good* or *confident*)

entries.related: *capable* — able, often with more potential; *proficient* — skilled through practice, more formal; *incompetent* — the opposite, a strong criticism.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An unfair situation in which some people have more money, rights or opportunities than others.
entries.usage: Common in news, economics and social science: *income / wealth / economic / gender inequality*, *rising inequality*, *inequality between rich and poor*. It is usually uncountable, but the plural is used for specific differences: *inequalities in health care*.
entries.pattern: income / wealth / gender inequality; inequality between A and B; inequalities in + area
examples: In some cities, life expectancy differs by fifteen years between rich and poor neighborhoods, a clear sign of **inequality**.
The economist's new book looks at how **inequality** has changed since the 1970s.
As kids, my brother and I complained loudly about the **inequality** of chores in our house.

drill.sentence: The report shows that the richest households keep pulling away from the poorest, so income {{inequality}} is rising.
drill.hint: an unfair difference between groups (not *disparity* or *gap*)

mistake.wrong: Unequality between rich and poor is growing.
mistake.right: Inequality between rich and poor is growing.
mistake.why: The adjective is *unequal*, but the noun takes *in-*: *inequality*.

entries.related: *disparity* — a large difference, more formal and neutral; *inequity* — unfairness, injustice; *equality* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Giving someone a wrong idea or impression, often without saying anything that is actually false.
entries.usage: Common in news, consumer complaints and law: *misleading advertising / claims / headlines / statistics*, *deeply / highly misleading*. It is softer than *false* or *a lie*, so *It's misleading to say…* is a polite way to dispute a claim. The verb is *mislead*, past *misled* (mis-LED).
entries.pattern: misleading information / claims / headlines; it's misleading to say (that)…
examples: The ad says “free breakfast,” which is **misleading**; it's only free if you stay three nights.
The chart is **misleading** because the vertical axis doesn't start at zero.
Calling the trail “easy” is a bit **misleading**, since the last mile is a steep climb.

drill.sentence: The store was fined for {{misleading}} ads that promised “free” phones but hid the monthly fees.
drill.hint: giving a wrong impression (not *deceptive*, *false* or *fake*)

entries.related: *deceptive* — likely to deceive, stronger; *inaccurate* — not correct; *disingenuous* — insincere, pretending not to know.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The period or situation that follows a bad event such as a war, disaster or crisis, including the effects it leaves.
entries.usage: Almost always *the aftermath of* + event or *in the aftermath (of)*: *in the aftermath of the storm*. It is common in news and history and refers to something negative; for a happy event like a wedding, say *after* or *the days after* instead. The stress is on the first syllable.
entries.pattern: in the aftermath of + disaster / crisis / war; the immediate aftermath
examples: In the **aftermath** of the hurricane, thousands of families had no power for weeks.
Kim wrote a memoir about her divorce and its messy **aftermath**.
In some towns, the **aftermath** of the 2008 financial crisis lasted for a decade.

drill.sentence: The town is still dealing with the {{aftermath}} of last spring's tornado, and dozens of families haven't moved back yet.
drill.hint: the difficult period after the disaster (not *effects*, *damage* or *fallout*)

entries.related: *in the wake of* — following, often as a result of; *fallout* — bad effects that come later; *repercussions* — unwanted results of an action.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The freedom or authority to decide what to do in a situation; also the ability to keep private information secret and avoid embarrassing people.
entries.usage: The first sense is common in fixed phrases: *at someone's discretion*, *use your discretion*, *have discretion over*. The second appears in *with discretion* and *count on someone's discretion*. German *Diskretion* has only the second meaning, so learners often miss phrases like *at the manager's discretion*.
entries.pattern: at someone's discretion; use your discretion; with (great) discretion
examples: Tipping is at your **discretion**, but most people here leave about twenty percent.
The judge has the **discretion** to reduce the sentence for a first offense.
I told my manager about my health problem, and I really appreciated her **discretion**.

drill.sentence: Late homework is accepted at the teacher's {{discretion}}, so it's worth asking politely.
drill.hint: if the teacher decides to allow it (not *choice*)

entries.related: *judgment* — the ability to make good decisions; *confidentiality* — keeping information secret, official; *discreet* — the adjective, careful not to reveal things.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To find new people and persuade them to join a company, organization, team or army.
entries.usage: Common in HR, sports, the military and volunteer work: *recruit staff / volunteers / players / members*, *recruit someone to do something*. In US college sports, *recruiting* high-school athletes is a major topic. In casual talk it is also used jokingly for getting friends to help: *I recruited my brothers to help me move*.
entries.pattern: recruit staff / volunteers / players; recruit someone to + verb; recruit from + place
examples: The hospital is trying to **recruit** more nurses by offering big signing bonuses.
I **recruited** my two brothers to carry the couch up four flights of stairs.
Top college football programs start **recruiting** players while they're still in high school.

drill.sentence: Every fall, the choir {{recruits}} new singers by performing at the student activities fair.
drill.hint: brings in new members (not *attracts* or *finds*)

entries.related: *hire* — give someone a paid job; *enlist* — get someone's help, or join the army; *headhunt* — recruit someone who works for another company.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Taking a lot of time, often more than you want to spend.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in everyday talk: *a time-consuming process / task / job*, *extremely time-consuming*. It is mildly negative and often paired with cost: *costly and time-consuming*. It is hyphenated both before a noun and after a verb (*It's time-consuming*).
entries.pattern: a time-consuming process / task; costly and time-consuming; too time-consuming to + verb
examples: Renewing a passport isn't hard, but it's **time-consuming**, so start well before your trip.
Making fresh pasta is fun, but it's too **time-consuming** for a weeknight dinner.
Lawsuits are costly and **time-consuming**, so most disputes are settled out of court.

drill.sentence: Sorting through thirty years of family photos turned out to be a slow, {{time-consuming}} job.
drill.hint: eating up many hours (not *tedious*, *painstaking* or *laborious*)

entries.related: *tedious* — long and boring; *labor-intensive* — needing a lot of work; *quick* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun (plural)
entries.meaning: Basic services supplied to a home or building, such as electricity, gas and water, and the monthly bills for them.
entries.usage: Very common in American housing talk: *Utilities are included*, *rent plus utilities*, *pay the utilities*, *a utility bill*. The companies that supply them are also called *utilities* or *utility companies*. Whether internet and trash pickup count depends on the landlord; British English more often says *bills* (*bills included*).
entries.pattern: utilities (are) included; rent plus utilities; a utility bill / company
examples: The apartment is $1,400 a month, and **utilities** are included.
Our **utilities** go way up in January because the house has old gas heating.
After the ice storm, crews from three **utilities** worked around the clock to restore power.

drill.sentence: The rent seems cheap, but you'll also pay about two hundred dollars a month in {{utilities}}.
drill.hint: power, water and gas (not *bills* or *fees*)

entries.related: *bills* — the everyday word, also the British choice; *amenities* — useful extras in a building, like a gym or laundry room; *services* — more general.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Feeling that there is too much to deal with, so that you cannot cope or think clearly.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, emails and health talk: *I'm feeling overwhelmed*, *overwhelmed with / by work*, *a little / completely overwhelmed*. It is an accepted, honest way to say you are struggling, softer than *I can't cope*. The verb *overwhelm* is often passive for systems too: *Hospitals were overwhelmed with patients*.
entries.pattern: feel overwhelmed; overwhelmed by / with + work / emails / choices
examples: Between the new baby and the move, we're feeling completely **overwhelmed** right now.
First-year students often feel **overwhelmed** by the amount of reading.
In my first American grocery store, I was **overwhelmed** by forty kinds of cereal.

drill.sentence: When I came back from vacation to 214 unread emails, I felt totally {{overwhelmed}}.
drill.hint: unable to cope with how much there was (not *swamped* or *stressed*)

entries.related: *swamped* — informal, very busy; *stressed (out)* — worried and tense; *burned out* — exhausted after a long period of stress.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A measure, usually a number, used to judge performance, progress or quality.
entries.usage: Very common in business, tech and management: *key metrics*, *a metric for success*, *track a metric*, *by any metric*. In casual talk it can sound like office jargon, and people say *measure* or just *number*. As an adjective, *metric* refers to the metric system, which Americans rarely use in daily life.
entries.pattern: a key metric; a metric for + noun; track / measure a metric; by any metric
examples: The main **metric** for the new app is how many people are still using it after a week.
By almost any **metric**, this was the team's best season in twenty years.
The hospital treats emergency room wait times as a key **metric** of patient care.

drill.sentence: Step count is a simple {{metric}}, but it doesn't tell you much about how fit you really are.
drill.hint: a figure used to judge progress (not *measure* or *indicator*)

entries.related: *measure* — more general, also everyday; *KPI* — key performance indicator, business jargon; *benchmark* — a standard to compare against.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To control an activity, business or industry with official rules, usually made and enforced by a government or agency.
entries.usage: Common in news, law and business: *regulate an industry / the market / the use of something*, *heavily / tightly regulated*. The passive is very frequent (*Drones are regulated by the FAA*). The nouns are *regulation* (a rule, often plural) and *regulator* (an official body).
entries.pattern: regulate an industry / the use of + noun; heavily / strictly regulated; be regulated by + agency
examples: The city now **regulates** short-term rentals, so owners need a permit to list on Airbnb.
In the US, drones are **regulated** by the Federal Aviation Administration.
Banks are among the most heavily **regulated** businesses in the country.

drill.sentence: Many states {{regulate}} how much interest payday lenders can charge, but the rules vary a lot.
drill.hint: set official rules for (not *control*, *limit*, *cap* or *restrict*)

entries.related: *control* — more general; *oversee* — watch and manage; *deregulate* — remove rules, the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To go to an expert or a source, such as a doctor, lawyer or reference book, for advice or information.
entries.usage: More formal than *ask* or *check*: *consult a doctor / a lawyer / a specialist*, *consult a map / the manual*. *Consult with* is common in American English when people discuss something together (*consult with the team*). *Consult your doctor before starting any exercise program* is a standard American warning.
entries.pattern: consult a doctor / lawyer / map / manual; consult with + people (about + topic)
examples: If the pain doesn't go away in a few days, **consult** a doctor.
I had to **consult** the manual three times just to set the clock on the microwave.
The mayor promised to **consult** with residents before changing any bus routes.

drill.sentence: Before signing the lease, it's smart to {{consult}} a lawyer about the cancellation terms.
drill.hint: go to for expert advice (not *ask*, *see* or *call*)

entries.related: *ask* — the everyday word; *seek advice from* — formal; *consultant* — a paid expert who advises companies.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Causing difficulties or full of problems, so that something does not work well or is hard to accept.
entries.usage: It sounds more analytical than *a problem* and is common in reports, meetings and reviews: *This approach is problematic because…*, *highly problematic*. Since the 2010s it has also been widely used to call jokes, words or behavior offensive or harmful (*a problematic joke*).
entries.pattern: be problematic (for + someone / because …); highly / deeply problematic
examples: Parking downtown is **problematic** on game days, so take the train.
Judging teachers by a single test score is **problematic**; it misses most of what they do.
Lending money to family can be **problematic**, so put the agreement in writing.

drill.sentence: Driving a big pickup truck through the narrow streets of the old town can be {{problematic}}.
drill.hint: causing difficulties (formal; not *tricky*, *difficult* or *challenging*)

entries.related: *tricky* — informal, hard to handle; *questionable* — doubtful, possibly wrong; *straightforward* — the opposite, simple and clear.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Easily broken or damaged; also weak and easily made worse, about health, peace, economies or feelings.
entries.usage: Literal on boxes and labels (*Fragile, handle with care*) and figurative in news: *a fragile peace / economy / recovery / truce*. About people it means weak in health or easily upset: *fragile health*, *a fragile ego*. Americans say FRAJ-ul, rhyming with American *agile*; British speakers say FRAJ-ile.
entries.pattern: a fragile vase / peace / economy / ego; fragile health
examples: Wrap the wine glasses in newspaper; they're very **fragile**.
After a week in the hospital, my grandfather is still pretty **fragile**.
The two neighbors have a **fragile** truce after last summer's fight over the fence.

drill.sentence: The economy is still {{fragile}}, so one bad month of job numbers could push it back into recession.
drill.hint: easily damaged (not *weak*, *shaky*, *unstable* or *vulnerable*)

entries.related: *delicate* — easily damaged, also fine and beautiful; *brittle* — hard but breaks easily; *sturdy* — the opposite, strong and solid.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The freedom to make your own decisions and act without being controlled by others.
entries.usage: Common at work (*give employees more autonomy*), in education, in medicine (*patient autonomy*) and in politics (*regional autonomy*). It sounds positive and a bit formal; in conversation people also say *independence* or *freedom*. The adjective *autonomous* is also used for self-driving cars and robots.
entries.pattern: have / give someone autonomy (over + area); patient / personal autonomy
examples: I love this job because I have real **autonomy**; nobody tells me how to plan my day.
Teenagers want more **autonomy**, but they still need their parents to drive them everywhere.
Doctors must respect a patient's **autonomy**, even when they disagree with the decision.

drill.sentence: After the stroke, Grandpa hated losing his {{autonomy}}; he couldn't even drive to the store by himself.
drill.hint: the ability to run his own life (not *independence* or *freedom*)

entries.related: *independence* — not depending on others; *self-determination* — a people's right to choose their own government; *micromanagement* — the opposite at work.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To be, or officially count as, a particular thing; also to be the parts that together form something.
entries.usage: Formal and common in law, rules and academic writing: *constitute a breach / a violation / a threat / a crime*. In the second sense, the parts are the subject (*Women constitute 60 percent of the staff*); with *consist of* and *comprise*, the whole is the subject. In conversation people say *be*, *count as* or *make up*.
entries.pattern: constitute a breach / violation / threat; parts + constitute + whole
examples: Sharing a customer's address without permission may **constitute** a breach of privacy law.
Does one late payment really **constitute** a pattern? The bank seems to think so.
Students over twenty-five now **constitute** about a third of the college's enrollment.

drill.sentence: Keeping a dog in the apartment, even for a weekend, would {{constitute}} a violation of your lease.
drill.hint: formal verb meaning *count as* in rules and law (not *represent* or *amount to*)

entries.related: *make up* — form the parts of a whole, everyday; *amount to* — be equal to, often negative; *comprise* — consist of, formal.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To accept or put up with something you dislike or disagree with, without trying to stop it or complaining.
entries.usage: Common at home, at school and at work, very often with a negative: *We will not tolerate bullying*, *I can't tolerate rudeness*. In conversation, *put up with* and *stand* are more casual. It also describes the body: *tolerate a medication*, *tolerate heat*.
entries.pattern: tolerate + noun / -ing; will not tolerate; can't tolerate
examples: The diner's owner doesn't **tolerate** rudeness toward her servers; she'll ask you to leave.
I've **tolerated** my roommate's dirty dishes in the sink for months, but I'm finally going to say something.
Jen **tolerated** her brother-in-law's jokes all through dinner for her sister's sake.

drill.sentence: The coach is easygoing, but he won't {{tolerate}} players showing up late to practice.
drill.hint: let it happen without complaint (not *accept*, *allow*, *stand* or *put up with*)

entries.related: *put up with* — informal, the most common in speech; *stand* — usually negative: *I can't stand it*; *tolerant* — adjective, accepting of differences.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make information known, especially information that was private or secret, often because a rule or law requires it.
entries.usage: Formal and common in law, finance, medicine and journalism: *disclose information / details / a conflict of interest*, *disclose something to someone*, *an undisclosed sum*. In conversation, *tell* or *reveal* is more natural. The noun is *disclosure*, and an NDA is a *nondisclosure agreement*.
entries.pattern: disclose information / details / the terms (to + someone); an undisclosed sum / location
examples: The company refused to **disclose** how much it paid for the building.
In many states, sellers must **disclose** any known water damage before they sell a house.
Your doctor can't **disclose** your medical records without your written consent.

drill.sentence: The two teams agreed on a trade, but neither side would {{disclose}} the terms to reporters.
drill.hint: make known officially (not *reveal*, *release*, *divulge* or *share*)

entries.related: *reveal* — make known, more general; *divulge* — reveal something secret, formal; *withhold* — the opposite, keep information back.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To treat people unfairly by using their work or weakness for your own advantage; or to use a resource or an opportunity fully.
entries.usage: The first sense is strongly critical: *exploit workers / children / someone's trust*. The second is neutral: *exploit natural resources / an opportunity / a weakness*; in security, attackers *exploit a bug*. The noun *exploit* (a daring act, or a security attack) is stressed on the first syllable: EK-sploit.
entries.pattern: exploit workers / someone's fear; exploit a resource / an opportunity / a weakness
examples: The factory **exploited** its workers, paying them almost nothing for twelve-hour shifts.
Scammers **exploit** people's fear by pretending to call from the IRS.
The region hopes to **exploit** its strong winds by building more wind farms.

drill.sentence: The striker was quick to {{exploit}} the goalkeeper's mistake and scored into an empty net.
drill.hint: use fully to his own advantage (not *punish*)

entries.related: *take advantage of* — the everyday equivalent for both senses; *capitalize on* — make good use of a chance; *manipulate* — control someone unfairly.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Famous or well known for something bad.
entries.usage: Use it only for negative reputations: *a notorious criminal*, *notorious for delays*, *notoriously difficult*. It is not a stronger word for *famous*: *a notorious singer* suggests scandal. German *notorisch* is closer to *chronic* or *habitual*: *ein notorischer Nörgler* is *a chronic complainer*.
entries.pattern: notorious for + noun / -ing; a notorious criminal / case; notoriously + adjective
examples: This intersection is **notorious** for accidents; three people were hurt here last year.
My uncle is **notorious** for showing up to family dinners two hours late.
Alcatraz once held some of America's most **notorious** criminals, including Al Capone.

drill.sentence: Our landlord is {{notorious}} for keeping deposits over the tiniest scratch, so take photos when you move in.
drill.hint: has a bad reputation (not *infamous*, *known* or *famous*)

mistake.why: *Notorious* means famous for something bad; for a good reputation, use *famous*, *renowned* or *well-known*.

entries.related: *infamous* — very close, often even stronger; *famous* — known for good or neutral reasons; *renowned* — famous and admired.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A detailed analysis and judgment of a piece of work, an idea or a theory, looking at both its strengths and its weaknesses.
entries.usage: Common in academic writing, journalism and art and design schools: *a critique of + book / idea / policy*, *write / offer a critique*, *a group critique*. Unlike *criticism*, it is not necessarily negative; it is a careful evaluation. German *Kritik* covers *criticism*, *critique* and *review*, but English *critic* is always a person.
entries.pattern: a (sharp / detailed / thoughtful) critique of + noun; give / write / offer a critique
examples: Her professor gave a detailed **critique** of her short story, with notes on almost every page.
The book is a sharp **critique** of how social media shapes teenagers' self-image.
In art school, every Friday ended with a group **critique** of our paintings.

drill.sentence: The article offers a thoughtful {{critique}} of the city's plan to replace the old library with condos.
drill.hint: detailed judgment of good and bad points (not *criticism*, *analysis* or *review*)

mistake.wrong: Thanks for your critic of my essay.
mistake.right: Thanks for your critique of my essay.
mistake.why: A *critic* is a person who judges work; the analysis itself is a *critique*.

entries.related: *criticism* — usually negative comments; *review* — a published judgment of a book, film or product; *critic* — the person who judges.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Too; more than is reasonable, necessary or helpful.
entries.usage: Used before adjectives, usually with a critical tone: *overly cautious / optimistic / sensitive / complicated*. *Not overly* is a common understatement for *not very* (*I'm not overly worried*). Some adjectives also have a one-word form with *over-* (*overcautious*, *overconfident*), but *overly* works with almost any adjective.
entries.pattern: overly + adjective (cautious / optimistic / complicated); not overly + adjective
examples: The instructions were **overly** complicated; it took us an hour to build a simple bookshelf.
I'm not **overly** worried about the exam; I've been studying for weeks.
Looking back, my parents were **overly** strict about TV; we got thirty minutes a day.

drill.sentence: My trainer says I'm being {{overly}} cautious and can easily lift ten more pounds.
drill.hint: more than necessary (not *too*, *unnecessarily* or *excessively*)

entries.related: *too* — the everyday word; *excessively* — formal, stronger; *unduly* — formal, more than is justified (*unduly harsh*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To suffer something difficult, painful or unpleasant, patiently and often for a long time.
entries.usage: More serious than *put up with*: *endure pain / hardship / a long winter / years of abuse*. In conversation it is often used humorously for small suffering (*I endured three hours of vacation photos*). Without an object it means *last for a long time* (*Their friendship endured*), which is formal; the adjective *enduring* means lasting.
entries.pattern: endure pain / hardship / delays / years of + noun
examples: She **endured** months of painful physical therapy before she could walk again.
We **endured** a four-hour delay on the runway with no food and no air conditioning.
I had to **endure** my brother-in-law's lecture on crypto for the entire dinner.

drill.sentence: My grandparents {{endured}} years of poverty after the war before they could buy a house of their own.
drill.hint: bore patiently for a long time (not *survived*, *suffered*, *lived through* or *weathered*)

entries.related: *put up with* — tolerate something annoying, informal; *withstand* — resist without being damaged; *bear* — accept something painful, often in *can't bear*.
